column31:
It felt like the music mostly hit the emotional changes on screen with its intensity and volume changes, but lacking in spacing and feel. 
The first movie, for example you could always feel it's whimsical and magical setting, but it didn't change much when going from the green and sunny path down to the dark and somber forest. It always felt like the main character was simply walking the dog peacefully. The piano is also constantly playing, instead of giving more space to make the viewer feel these changes. 
In the second movie it made more sense due to the natural genre of the film, but still the intensity and volume were a lot more noticeable as opposed to the pacing and the melody that should acompany each action. 
On the third film it was mostly a piano playing over a film, nothing that would be really relating the picture to music, but the soundtrack was more pleasant to hear.

column31:
Not sure about the methodology and validity of this survey. We know that it's AI generated music, so our listening is already biased. On the quality of the generated soundtracks, they are all hopelessly bad, and the variation between them is minimal. It is impossible to compare the fit with the film excerpts  between the two proposed soundtracks. They are too similar.

I don't see any useful insight coming from the data collected through this survey. I would suggest a different survey, with a question to evaluate soundtracks, without declaring how they were created, and have a human-made one in the mix as a reference and benchmark. In this case probably better to have 4-5 soundtracks for the same excerpt  generated in different ways and with different instrumentations.

It's something that needed a slower tempo to emphasize tension, which both tracks were too joyful and fast paced, to create a sensation of fear. Obviously movie soundtracks are full of other instruments to add dynamism and richness to the scenes, but the moods needs to fit the scene, which by itself, it's a wonderful form of art.
